claim: Overexpression of anti-apoptotic proteins MCL1 and Bcl-xL are frequently observed in many cancers.
source: Overexpression of anti-apoptotic proteins MCL1 and Bcl-xL are frequently observed in many cancers.
evidence: This is a general statement about cancer biology presented in the abstract without specific data in this manuscript, but is supported by the broader scientific literature.

claim: Inhibitors targeting MCL1 are in clinical development.
source: Inhibitors targeting MCL1 are in clinical development, however numerous cancer models are intrinsically resistant to this approach.
evidence: Referenced in the context of the study and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Numerous cancer models are intrinsically resistant to MCL1 inhibition.
source: Inhibitors targeting MCL1 are in clinical development, however numerous cancer models are intrinsically resistant to this approach.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript showing resistant cell lines.

claim: Genome-wide CRISPR screens identified three components (CUL5, RNF7 and UBE2F) of a cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase complex (CRL5) that resensitized cells to MCL1 inhibition.
source: Remarkably, both screens identified three components (CUL5, RNF7 and UBE2F) of a cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase complex (CRL5) that resensitized cells to MCL1 inhibition.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the screen data shown in Figure 2 and validated in subsequent experiments.

claim: Levels of the BH3-only pro-apoptotic proteins Bim and Noxa are proteasomally regulated by the CRL5 complex.
source: We find that levels of the BH3-only pro-apoptotic proteins Bim and Noxa are proteasomally regulated by the CRL5 complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 4 showing increased Bim and Noxa levels upon CRL5 depletion and proteasome inhibitor experiments.

claim: Accumulation of Noxa caused by depletion of CRL5 components was responsible for re-sensitization to CDK9 inhibitor, but not MCL1 inhibitor.
source: Accumulation of Noxa caused by depletion of CRL5 components was responsible for re-sensitization to CDK9 inhibitor, but not MCL1 inhibitor.
evidence: This is supported by epistasis experiments shown in Figure 5 where Noxa knockdown prevented CDK9i-induced apoptosis in CUL5-depleted cells but not MCL1i-induced apoptosis.

claim: Cancer cells frequently manipulate the intrinsic apoptotic pathway to evade cell death and expand their proliferative capacity.
source: Cancer cells frequently manipulate the intrinsic apoptotic pathway to evade cell death and expand their proliferative capacity.
evidence: This is a general statement about cancer biology supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Aberrant increases in levels of anti-apoptotic proteins in the BCL-2 family have been widely implicated in the transformation of cancer cells and the development of resistance to current therapies.
source: Aberrant increases in levels of anti-apoptotic proteins in the BCL-2 family, such as amplification of MCL1, have been widely implicated in the transformation of cancer cells and the development of resistance to current therapies (Kelly and Strasser, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kelly and Strasser, 2011.

claim: Multi-domain proteins BAK, BAX and BOK serve as apoptosis executors in the mitochondria.
source: BCL-2 family members are classified based on the conservation of their BCL-2 homology (BH) domains: multi-domain proteins BAK, BAX and BOK serve as apoptosis executors in the mitochondria
evidence: This is established knowledge about BCL-2 family protein function.

claim: Proteins containing only the BH3 domain (BH3-only) promote BAK/BAX activation.
source: proteins containing only the BH3 domain (BH3-only) promote BAK/BAX activation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of apoptosis regulation.

claim: Anti-apoptotic proteins such as MCL1, Bcl-xL and BCL-2 inhibit apoptosis by antagonistic binding to pro-apoptotic BH3-only proteins as well as BAK and BAX.
source: Anti-apoptotic proteins such as MCL1, Bcl-xL and BCL-2 inhibit apoptosis by antagonistic binding to pro-apoptotic BH3-only proteins as well as BAK and BAX (Czabotar et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Czabotar et al., 2014.

claim: Gene amplification of MCL1 and BCL2L1 (Bcl-xL) are key determinants of survival in many cancers, including breast cancer, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), multiple myeloma, acute myeloid leukemia, and B-cell acute lymphoblatic leukemia.
source: High-resolution investigation of somatic copy number alterations has revealed that gene amplification of MCL1 and BCL2L1 (Bcl-xL) are key determinants of survival in many cancers, including breast cancer, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), multiple myeloma, acute myeloid leukemia, and B-cell acute lymphoblatic leukemia (Goodwin et al., 2015; Koss et al., 2013; Xiao et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Amplification of MCL1 is a prognostic indicator for disease severity and progression.
source: Amplification of MCL1 is a prognostic indicator for disease severity and progression, making it an attractive therapeutic target (Campbell et al., 2018; Yin et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Campbell et al., 2018 and Yin et al., 2016.

claim: The first BH3-mimetics that specifically antagonized Bcl-xL were associated with significant thrombocytopenia.
source: Unfortunately, the first BH3-mimetics that specifically antagonized Bcl-xL were associated with significant thrombocytopenia, thus complicating their therapeutic use (Lessene et al., 2013; Leverson et al., 2015a; Tao et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Compounds that selectively target MCL1 are currently in clinical trials.
source: Small-molecule inhibition of MCL1 has recently gained significant attention (Figure 1A), and compounds that selectively target MCL1 are currently in clinical trials (Abulwerdi et al., 2014; Burke et al., 2015; Caenepeel et al., 2018; Kotschy et al., 2016; Leverson et al., 2015b; Tron et al., 2018; Phase I Study of S64315 Administred Intravenously in Patients With Acute Myeloid Leukaemia or Myelodysplastic Syndrome).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including a clinical trial reference.

claim: Direct BH3-mimetic MCL1 inhibitors show potent efficacy with low cytotoxicity in preclinical hematological malignancies.
source: Promising reports of direct BH3-mimetic MCL1 inhibitors in preclinical hematological malignancies show potent efficacy with low cytotoxicity (Kotschy et al., 2016; Leverson et al., 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kotschy et al., 2016 and Leverson et al., 2015b.

claim: MCL1 inhibitors showed little single agent activity in solid breast tumors unless combined with a chemotherapeutic agent.
source: However, assessment of MCL1 inhibitors in solid breast tumors showed little single agent activity unless combined with a chemotherapeutic agent (Merino et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Merino et al., 2017.

claim: CDK9 inhibition restricts transcription elongation.
source: CDK9 inhibition restricts transcription elongation thus exploiting all mRNAs and proteins that have short-lived half-lives.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CDK9 function, also illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: MCL1 is particularly susceptible to acute CDK9i treatment due to its short half-life.
source: Due to its short half-life, MCL1 is one of several targets that is particularly susceptible to acute CDK9i treatment, and other (proto-)oncogenes such as MYC are also CDK9i targets (Figure 1A) (Akgul et al., 2000; Gregory et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2014a; Lemke et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: CDK9 inhibition does not affect levels of other anti-apoptotic proteins such as Bcl-xL.
source: Although CDK9 inhibition suppresses MCL1 expression, it does not affect levels of other anti-apoptotic proteins such as Bcl-xL, exposing a potential vulnerability in CDK9i treatment such that cancers may already have or develop a mode of resistance.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Selective CDK9 inhibitors have shown promising results in preclinical murine models.
source: Selective CDK9 inhibitors have shown promising results in preclinical murine models; however, they have a limited therapeutic window and must be acutely dosed for clinical applications due to their global effects on transcription (Garcia-Cuellar et al., 2014; Hellvard et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Garcia-Cuellar et al., 2014 and Hellvard et al., 2016.

claim: CDK9 inhibitors have a limited therapeutic window and must be acutely dosed for clinical applications due to their global effects on transcription.
source: Selective CDK9 inhibitors have shown promising results in preclinical murine models; however, they have a limited therapeutic window and must be acutely dosed for clinical applications due to their global effects on transcription (Garcia-Cuellar et al., 2014; Hellvard et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and by the experimental design of the study which uses acute dosing.

claim: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer mortality.
source: As lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer mortality and most NSCLC patients develop resistance to first-line treatment, we performed genome-wide CRISPR inhibition (CRISPRi) screens in a NSCLC line resistant to both CDK9 and MCL1 inhibition (Siegel et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Siegel et al., 2016.

claim: Most NSCLC patients develop resistance to first-line treatment.
source: As lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer mortality and most NSCLC patients develop resistance to first-line treatment, we performed genome-wide CRISPR inhibition (CRISPRi) screens in a NSCLC line resistant to both CDK9 and MCL1 inhibition (Siegel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a general clinical observation supported by the citation.

claim: Several cell lines with amplified MCL1 (copy number ≥3) were highly sensitive to CDK9i and MCL1i.
source: Several cell lines with amplified MCL1 (copy number ≥3) were highly sensitive to CDK9i and MCL1i, consistent with overexpression of MCL1 to escape apoptosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 1B and Table 1.

claim: Several NSCLC lines were resistant to CDK9i and MCL1i despite being MCL1-amplified.
source: We also found several NSCLC lines resistant to CDK9i and MCL1i despite being MCL1-amplified.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 1B and Table 1.

claim: Increased Bcl-xL expression correlated with the MCL1-amplified lines that were resistant to CDK9i and MCL1i.
source: Increased Bcl-xL expression correlated with the MCL1-amplified lines that were resistant to CDK9i and MCL1i.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 1B and Table 1 showing MCL1:Bcl-xL ratios.

claim: MCL1-amplified cell lines with low levels of Bcl-xL were sensitive to CDK9i and MCL1i.
source: Conversely, MCL1-amplified cell lines with low levels of Bcl-xL were sensitive to CDK9i and MCL1i.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 1B and Table 1.

claim: Both MCL1i and CDK9i induce apoptosis and cell death in a sensitive cell line (H23) after just 6 hr, with saturated cell death and caspase activation at 1 μM.
source: Both MCL1i and CDK9i induce apoptosis and cell death in a sensitive cell line (H23) after just 6 hr, with saturated cell death and caspase activation at 1 μM.
evidence: This claim is supported by the dose response curves shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A resistant line (LK2) was about 100-fold more resistant to CDK9i and MCL1i compared to the sensitive H23 line.
source: Conversely, a resistant line (LK2) was about 100-fold more resistant to CDK9i and MCL1i (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the dose response curves shown in Figure 1C.

claim: After extended treatment (24 hr), CDK9i induced a significant decrease in cell viability in both the resistant and sensitive cell lines.
source: After extended treatment (24 hr), CDK9i induced a significant decrease in cell viability in both the resistant and sensitive cell lines, highlighting off-target toxicity presumably stemming from global transcriptional arrest independent of targeting short half-life transcripts such as MCL1 and MYC (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cell viability data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Extended CDK9i treatment causes off-target toxicity presumably stemming from global transcriptional arrest independent of targeting short half-life transcripts such as MCL1 and MYC.
source: After extended treatment (24 hr), CDK9i induced a significant decrease in cell viability in both the resistant and sensitive cell lines, highlighting off-target toxicity presumably stemming from global transcriptional arrest independent of targeting short half-life transcripts such as MCL1 and MYC (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 1D, involving inference about the mechanism.

claim: Prolonged CDK9i treatment induces non-specific cell death, possibly due to its polypharmacology.
source: Prolonged CDK9i treatment induces non-specific cell death, possibly due to its polypharmacology, and so a growth-based screen measuring cell abundance after extended compound exposure was inappropriate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data in Figure 1D and knowledge of CDK9 function.

claim: Knockdown of Bcl-xL led to re-sensitization of LK2 cells to CDK9i and MCL1i.
source: We found multiple sgRNAs targeting Bcl-xL led to re-sensitization of LK2 cells to CDK9i and MCL1i (Figure 2B–C), confirming reports that depletion of both MCL1 and Bcl-xL initiates apoptosis (Goodwin et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by the screen data shown in Figure 2B-C and by citations.

claim: Depletion of both MCL1 and Bcl-xL initiates apoptosis.
source: We found multiple sgRNAs targeting Bcl-xL led to re-sensitization of LK2 cells to CDK9i and MCL1i (Figure 2B–C), confirming reports that depletion of both MCL1 and Bcl-xL initiates apoptosis (Goodwin et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and confirmed by the screen data.

claim: Downregulation of the mitochondrial porin VDAC2 promoted apoptosis in drug-treated cells.
source: Downregulation of the mitochondrial porin VDAC2 also promoted apoptosis in drug-treated cells (Figure 2B–C), consistent with its proposed role in BAK/BAX sequestration at the mitochondrial membrane (Cheng et al., 2003; Chin et al., 2018; Lauterwasser et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by the screen data shown in Figure 2B-C and by citations.

claim: VDAC2 has a proposed role in BAK/BAX sequestration at the mitochondrial membrane.
source: Downregulation of the mitochondrial porin VDAC2 also promoted apoptosis in drug-treated cells (Figure 2B–C), consistent with its proposed role in BAK/BAX sequestration at the mitochondrial membrane (Cheng et al., 2003; Chin et al., 2018; Lauterwasser et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: EIF4G2 (DAP5) was identified as a hit in the CDK9i screen.
source: EIF4G2 (DAP5) was identified as a hit in the CDK9i screen (Figure 2B), and this gene has been implicated in stimulating cap-independent translation of anti-apoptotic protein BCL-2 (Marash et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by the screen data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: EIF4G2 has been implicated in stimulating cap-independent translation of anti-apoptotic protein BCL-2.
source: EIF4G2 (DAP5) was identified as a hit in the CDK9i screen (Figure 2B), and this gene has been implicated in stimulating cap-independent translation of anti-apoptotic protein BCL-2 (Marash et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Marash et al., 2008.

claim: The CDK9i screen had many more hits than the MCL1i screen.
source: Comparing the most significantly enriched genes from both screens showed an overlap between MCL1i and CDK9i. The CDK9i screen had many more hits, consistent with its polypharmacology of transcriptional inhibition (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the Venn diagram shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Significantly more of the top resensitization hits were shared between CDK9i and MCL1i than are expected by chance.
source: Despite separate mechanisms of drug action and potentially distinct targets, significantly more of the top resensitization hits were shared between CDK9i and MCL1i than are expected by chance (exact hypergeometric test p<6.4×10−9).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the screen data.

claim: Knockdown of multiple components of the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 3 (eIF-3) complex (EIF3H and EIF3M) resensitize LK2 cells to CDK9i and MCL1i.
source: First, knockdown of multiple components of the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 3 (eIF-3) complex (EIF3H and EIF3M) resensitize LK2 cells to CDK9i and MCL1i (Figure 2B–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the screen data shown in Figure 2B-C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: eIF-3 is reported to bind a highly specific program of messenger RNAs involved in cell proliferation and apoptosis.
source: eIF-3 is reported to bind a highly specific program of messenger RNAs involved in cell proliferation and apoptosis (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2015.

claim: CUL5 serves as a protein scaffold in the CRL5 complex, forming a platform for RNF7, UBE2F, Elongin B/C, and a substrate adaptor to recruit and ubiquitinate a target substrate.
source: CUL5 serves as a protein scaffold in the CRL5 complex, forming a platform for RNF7, UBE2F, Elongin B/C, and a substrate adaptor to recruit and ubiquitinate a target substrate (Figure 3A) (Kamura et al., 2004) (Huang et al., 2009) (Mahrour et al., 2008; Okumura et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: CUL5 and RNF7 appeared to be dependent on each other for stability such that when either protein was knocked down, levels of the corresponding protein were also diminished.
source: CUL5 and RNF7 appeared to be dependent on each other for stability such that when either protein was knocked down, levels of the corresponding protein were also diminished (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Depletion of UBE2F resulted in the disappearance of a higher molecular weight band corresponding to neddylated CUL5.
source: Depletion of UBE2F resulted in the disappearance of a higher molecular weight band corresponding to neddylated CUL5 (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Depletion of CUL5, RNF7, UBE2F or Bcl-xL significantly induced PARP cleavage when combined with CDK9i or MCL1i.
source: Assessing cleaved PARP (c-PARP) levels, we found that depletion of CUL5, RNF7, UBE2F or Bcl-xL significantly induced PARP cleavage when combined with CDK9i or MCL1i (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In the absence of drug, knockdown of Bcl-xL alone led to substantial apoptosis but this was not the case for knockdown of CUL5, RNF7 or UBE2F.
source: In the absence of drug, knockdown of Bcl-xL alone led to substantial apoptosis but this was not the case for knockdown of CUL5, RNF7 or UBE2F (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: Inactivation of CRL5 could be less toxic than inhibition of Bcl-xL.
source: This suggests that inactivation of CRL5 could be less toxic than inhibition of Bcl-xL and that inhibition of CRL5 may be better suited to co-administration with CDK9 and MCL1 inhibitors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that CRL5 depletion alone does not cause apoptosis while Bcl-xL depletion does.

claim: Challenging CUL5 or UBE2F knockout cells with CDK9i or MCL1i induced high levels of apoptosis at 1 μM of either compound, whereas wild type cells showed no response even at 10 μM.
source: Challenging CUL5 or UBE2F knockout cells with CDK9i or MCL1i induced high levels of apoptosis at 1 μM of either compound, whereas wild type cells showed no response even at 10 μM (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the dose response data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Drug treatment greatly reduced colony-forming ability in the CUL5 and UBE2F knockout cells.
source: Drug treatment greatly reduced colony-forming ability in the CUL5 and UBE2F knockout cells, indicating efficient and persistent resensitization of these cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the clonogenic assay data shown in Figure 3G-H.

claim: Individual knockdown of Elongin B by CRISPRi-induced apoptosis at levels similar to that of CUL5 knockdown.
source: Individual knockdown of Elongin B by CRISPRi-induced apoptosis at levels similar to that of CUL5 knockdown, but knockdown of Elongin C had minimal effect (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: Knockdown of Elongin C had minimal effect on apoptosis.
source: Individual knockdown of Elongin B by CRISPRi-induced apoptosis at levels similar to that of CUL5 knockdown, but knockdown of Elongin C had minimal effect (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: Elongin B and C have a potential separation of function.
source: Elongin B and C have often been described as functioning in a complex, but our results suggest a potential separation of function (Okumura et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of Elongin B and C knockdown.

claim: None of the literature-proposed substrate adaptors analyzed induced apoptosis following CDK9i or MCL1i treatment.
source: None of the literature-proposed substrate adaptors analyzed induced apoptosis following CDK9i or MCL1i treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and Figure 3—source data 1), but we cannot rule out redundancy between substrate adaptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Loss of CUL5 did not lead to accumulation of p53.
source: p53, a master regulator of apoptosis, can be a target of CRL5 during viral infection (Cai et al., 2006; Querido et al., 2001; Sato et al., 2009). However, loss of CUL5 did not lead to accumulation of p53 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D), nor affected MCL1 and Bcl-xL levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Loss of CUL5 did not affect MCL1 and Bcl-xL levels.
source: However, loss of CUL5 did not lead to accumulation of p53 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D), nor affected MCL1 and Bcl-xL levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Noxa was recently proposed to be a substrate of CRL5.
source: Pro-apoptotic proteins are required for efficient induction of cell death, and CRL5 could target pro-apoptotic proteins for proteasomal degradation. Indeed, Noxa was recently proposed to be a substrate of CRL5 (Zhou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2017.

claim: Knockdown of CRL5 components increased protein levels of two BH3-only proteins, Noxa and Bim.
source: Knockdown of CRL5 components increased protein levels of two BH3-only proteins, Noxa and Bim (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: After treatment with CDK9i or MCL1i, CUL5 knockdown had increased levels of both proapoptotic proteins Noxa and Bim while all other BH3-only proteins remained unchanged.
source: After treatment with CDK9i or MCL1i, we also found that CUL5 knockdown had increased levels of both proapoptotic proteins Noxa and Bim while all other BH3-only proteins remained unchanged (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: CDK9i treatment alone reduced levels of Noxa and Bim through transcriptional downregulation.
source: Interestingly, CDK9i treatment alone reduced levels of Noxa and Bim through transcriptional downregulation, presumably related to the half-lives of these mRNAs (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4B-D.

claim: Knockdown of CUL5 together with CDK9i rescued protein levels of Noxa and Bim but not mRNA levels, consistent with CRL5-mediated post-translational degradation of Noxa and Bim.
source: Knockdown of CUL5 together with CDK9i rescued protein levels of Noxa and Bim but not mRNA levels, consistent CRL5-mediated post-translational degradation of Noxa and Bim.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4B-D.

claim: Folimycin treatment did not affect the abundance of Noxa or Bim.
source: Folimycin treatment did not affect the abundance of Noxa or Bim (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Epoxomicin treatment causes accumulation of Bim in LK2 parental cells.
source: However, epoxomicin treatment causes accumulation of Bim in LK2 parental cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Epoxomicin treatment had no additional effect on Bim in CUL5 knockout cells.
source: Epoxomicin treatment had no additional effect on Bim in CUL5 knockout cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Under these conditions CRL5 appears to be the primary ligase for Bim.
source: Hence, under these conditions CRL5 appears to be the primary ligase for Bim.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that epoxomicin has no additional effect on Bim in CUL5 knockout cells.

claim: Noxa accumulates in both parental and CUL5 knockout cells after epoxomicin treatment.
source: Noxa accumulates in both parental and CUL5 knockout cells after epoxomicin treatment (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Noxa is proteasomally regulated.
source: These data indicate that Noxa is proteasomally regulated, but suggest that Noxa can be targeted by additional ubiquitin ligases.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Noxa accumulates after epoxomicin treatment.

claim: Noxa can be targeted by additional ubiquitin ligases beyond CRL5.
source: These data indicate that Noxa is proteasomally regulated, but suggest that Noxa can be targeted by additional ubiquitin ligases.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Noxa still accumulates after epoxomicin treatment in CUL5 knockout cells.

claim: Knocking down BAK prevented apoptosis induced by CDK9i or MCL1i in CUL5-CRISPRi cells.
source: If induction of apoptosis in CUL5-deficient cells requires Noxa and/or Bim, then removal of either or both factors should make the cells re-resistant to CDK9i and MCL1i. Knocking down BAK, the apoptosis effector required for cell death, prevented apoptosis induced by CDK9i or MCL1i in CUL5-CRISPRi cells (Figure 5A–B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Knocking down Noxa in CUL5-CRISPRi cells almost completely prevented CDK9i-induced apoptosis.
source: Knocking down Noxa in CUL5-CRISPRi cells almost completely prevented CDK9i-induced apoptosis (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Knocking down Bim in CUL5-CRISPRi cells did not prevent CDK9i-induced apoptosis.
source: Knocking down Bim in CUL5-CRISPRi cells did not prevent CDK9i-induced apoptosis, and simultaneously knocking down both Noxa and Bim in CUL5-CRISPRi cells did not further inhibit apoptosis beyond what was observed with knockdown of Noxa alone.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In CDK9i-treated cells lacking CUL5, initiation of apoptosis is primarily dependent on Noxa.
source: These data indicate that in CDK9i-treated cells lacking CUL5, initiation of apoptosis is primarily dependent on Noxa.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the epistasis experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Knocking down Noxa and/or Bim in CUL5-CRISPRi cells exposed to MCL1i still led to high levels of apoptosis.
source: Surprisingly, knocking down Noxa and/or Bim in CUL5-CRISPRi cells exposed to MCL1i still led to high levels of apoptosis (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The difference in apoptotic dependence between MCL1i and CDK9i could be due to transcriptional downregulation of Noxa and Bim during CDK9i or from downregulation of other pro-apoptotic factors.
source: The difference in apoptotic dependence between MCL1i and CDK9i could be due to transcriptional downregulation of Noxa and Bim during CDK9i (Figure 4D) or from downregulation of other pro-apoptotic factors, whose loss in conjunction with Noxa depletion leads to abrogation of apoptosis.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed differences.

claim: Depletion of key components of the CRL5 family of ubiquitin ligases sensitizes otherwise resistant cells to CDK9 and MCL1 inhibition.
source: In conclusion, we find that depletion of key components of the CRL5 family of ubiquitin ligases sensitizes otherwise resistant cells to CDK9 and MCL1 inhibition.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: The CRL5 complex targets pro-apoptotic proteins Noxa and Bim for degradation.
source: We show that the CRL5 complex targets pro-apoptotic proteins Noxa and Bim for degradation, and increased Noxa abundance upon CRL5 knockdown/out contributes to CDK9i sensitivity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by the data in Figure 4.

claim: Increased Noxa abundance upon CRL5 knockdown/out contributes to CDK9i sensitivity.
source: We show that the CRL5 complex targets pro-apoptotic proteins Noxa and Bim for degradation, and increased Noxa abundance upon CRL5 knockdown/out contributes to CDK9i sensitivity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by the epistasis experiments in Figure 5.

claim: Cullin-RING complexes comprise the largest class of ubiquitin ligases.
source: Cullin-RING complexes comprise the largest class of ubiquitin ligases and regulate a diverse array of biological processes (Petroski and Deshaies, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: CUL3 is implicated in a wide array of cancer biologies.
source: While CUL3 is implicated in a wide array of cancer biologies, relatively little is known about the physiological functions of many CUL5-containing ubiquitin ligases.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Relatively little is known about the physiological functions of many CUL5-containing ubiquitin ligases.
source: While CUL3 is implicated in a wide array of cancer biologies, relatively little is known about the physiological functions of many CUL5-containing ubiquitin ligases.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: A few reports have implicated genetic alterations in CUL5 in cancer progression.
source: A few reports have implicated genetic alterations in CUL5 in cancer progression and our unbiased screens reveal that the CUL5-RNF7-UBE2F ubiquitin ligase can modulate the apoptotic threshold of LK2 cells in response to multiple emerging cancer therapeutics (Burnatowska-Hledin et al., 2004; Fay et al., 2003; Lubbers et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The CUL5-RNF7-UBE2F ubiquitin ligase can modulate the apoptotic threshold of LK2 cells in response to multiple emerging cancer therapeutics.
source: A few reports have implicated genetic alterations in CUL5 in cancer progression and our unbiased screens reveal that the CUL5-RNF7-UBE2F ubiquitin ligase can modulate the apoptotic threshold of LK2 cells in response to multiple emerging cancer therapeutics (Burnatowska-Hledin et al., 2004; Fay et al., 2003; Lubbers et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Patients with lung cancers that exhibit loss of function mutations in either CUL5, RNF7, UBE2F or Elongin B that coincide with high expression of MCL1/Bcl-xL could be good candidates for treatment with CDK9i or MCL1i.
source: Based on our data, patients with lung cancers that exhibit loss of function mutations in either CUL5, RNF7, UBE2F or Elongin B that coincide with high expression of MCL1/Bcl-xL could be good candidates for treatment with CDK9i or MCL1i.
evidence: This is a clinical implication inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: There are currently no small-molecule inhibitors that target specific components of the CRL5 complex.
source: There are currently no small-molecule inhibitors that target specific components of the CRL5 complex.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of drug development.

claim: MLN4924 inhibits the NEDD8 activating enzyme (NAE), thereby preventing conjugation of NEDD8 onto all cullin scaffolds, and shows significant antitumor activity in clinical trials.
source: MLN4924 inhibits the NEDD8 activating enzyme (NAE), thereby preventing conjugation of NEDD8 onto all cullin scaffolds, and shows significant antitumor activity in clinical trials (Soucy et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Treatment with MLN7243, a small molecule inhibitor of the ubiquitin activating enzyme (UAE) currently in clinical trials, depletes cellular ubiquitin conjugates and demonstrates antitumor activity in xenografts.
source: Similiarly, treatment with MLN7243, a small molecule inhibitor of the ubiquitin activating enzyme (UAE) currently in clinical trials, depletes cellular ubiquitin conjugates and also demonstrates antitumor activity in xenografts (Hyer et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Clinically approved proteasome inhibitors such as bortezomib and carfilzomib are currently used in the treatment of multiple myeloma and lymphomas.
source: Several clinically approved proteasome inhibitors such as bortezomib and carfilzomib are currently used in the treatment of multiple myeloma and lymphomas (Kuhn et al., 2007; Richardson et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Patients experience adverse side effects due to the widespread effects of proteasome inhibition, complicating the possibility of co-dosing with CDK9i or MCL1i.
source: Although a therapeutic window exists for these compounds, patients also experience adverse side effects due to the widespread effects of proteasome inhibition, complicating the possibility of co-dosing with CDK9i or MCL1i.
evidence: This is a clinical consideration based on known side effects of proteasome inhibitors.

claim: The small molecule CC0651 selectively inhibits Cdc34A, an E2 for SCF-type CRLs, and has been shown to impede proliferation of cancer cells.
source: The small molecule CC0651 selectively inhibits Cdc34A, an E2 for SCF-type CRLs, and has been shown to impede proliferation of cancer cells (Ceccarelli et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: A potent inhibitor (ligand 7) targeting the von Hippel-Landau (VHL) substrate adaptor prevents the degradation of HIF-1α, a potential treatment for chronic anemia.
source: Another example is the synthesis of a potent inhibitor (ligand 7) targeting the von Hippel-Landau (VHL) substrate adaptor, thereby preventing the degradation of HIF-1α, a potential treatment for chronic anemia (Galdeano et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Targeting CRL5 could be used to combat innate and acquired resistance to therapeutics that directly or indirectly affect MCL1.
source: Our results in LK2 cells suggest that targeting CRL5 could be used to combat innate and acquired resistance to therapeutics that directly or indirectly affect MCL1.
evidence: This is a therapeutic implication inferred from the experimental findings.
